newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week- UK growth fears to take hold.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week- UK growth fears to take hold.

text.p: UK gilts look set to linger at lower levels this week as the pound keeps climbing and worries gather that Britain's economy is overheating and will need a substantial rate hike after the election, analysts said.

Gilts, down nearly five percent since February, looked likely to suffer all week as election jitters intensify, with no fundamental data out until UK industrial output on Wednesday and US retail sales figures on Friday.

"The approach of the election is likely to throw up something interesting," said analyst Steve Scott at Kleinwort Benson. "But it's a fairly quiet week for data -- there's not much to provide the UK with volatility."
He said gilts were losing out to Bunds as sterling rallied close to 4-1/2 year highs against the mark on Monday, prompting transfers from UK to German debt.
The gilt/Bund spread has widened to 185 points from 178 last week. Analysts said they saw no sign of it narrowing this week.

"If sterling carries on going up and people expect base rates to rise more quickly and by a larger amount than they did before, then there's a danger overseas investors will take profits in gilts," said Scott.
The nervous start to the week was not helped by a report in the Sunday Times suggesting official figures underestimated Britain's growth rate.

Author Michael Dicks, UK economist at Lehman Brothers, said GDP could actually be growing by more than four percent a year, rather than the 2.6 percent official figures show. That could require base rates to rise to eight percent from six, he said.
"I think some people may think that's rather high," said Scott. "There's a trend at the moment for city analysts to call interest rates higher, and that unsettles the market."
The report put pressure on Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George, due to discuss monetary policy at their monthly meeting on Thursday.
However analysts polled by Reuters said they expected rates to be left unchanged at 6.0 percent, as a move before the May 1 election would be "political suicide".

John Major's ruling Conservatives, traditionally favoured by financial markets, are widely expected to lose the election to the main opposition Labour Party, which has a lead of 20 percentage points and more in opinion polls.

Political backbiting intensified after last week's manifesto launches, as the Conservatives, dogged by sleaze issues, accused Labour of U-turning on several policies including possible entry to a single European currency.
With a Labour victory already priced in as a foregone conclusion, any sign of the Conservatives closing the gap will hit gilts as it would raise the prospect of a hung parliament.

"A hung parliament would be a nightmare scenario," said Mees Pierson broker Jonathon York. "If the Tories started to come back in the polls and squeezed Labour's lead to 5-10 percent, then gilts would get hurt quite a bit as given the margin of error it would be possible to see a tie in the election."

UK industrial production data for February will be released at 0830 GMT on Wednesday. Recent surveys showed domestic demand is boosting output, compensating for the effect of sterling's strength on exports. But the figures are not forecast as strong.
Economists forecast only a 0.3 percent increase in manufacturing output in February.
Housing starts for February, to be released at the same time could confirm the robustness of the residential property market, but were not likely to be market moving.
"I don't think Wednesday's figures will be too market sensitive unless they're way out of line, and they've been reasonably flat recently," said York.
Analysts put support for the June gilt future at 108-00. It was trading at 108-17 midway through Monday's session.
"As long as we hold above 108-00 the gilt market looks in reasonable shape," said York.
